cards.explanation: The answer is a celebration every single year. Mordecai, the Jew who wrote the letters, sets up an "annual celebration" on the fourteenth and fifteenth days of Adar (Esther 9:21). Annual means it comes around again and again. He didn't plan a party for one afternoon, friends. He put it on the calendar in ink.

The answer is joy. Mordecai writes that this is "…the month in which their sorrow turned to joy and their mourning into a holiday." Think about that swap, friends. Sorrow walked in the door and joy walked out wearing its coat. These days were set up to remember that turn.

The answer is True. Mordecai wrote "…that these were to be days of feasting and joy, of sending gifts to one another and to the poor." So the party doesn't stay at your own table, friends. It reaches your neighbors and the poor too. That's a celebration with the front door wide open.

The answer is False. The text says, "So the Jews agreed to continue the custom they had started, as Mordecai had written to them." (Esther 9:23). They had already started the custom, and they agreed to continue it. Agreeing is the opposite of refusing, friends.

The answer is a lot. The text says Haman son of Hammedatha, the Agagite, "…had cast the Pur (that is, the lot)…" Casting a lot is like pulling a name out of a hat, friends. Haman used it as part of his plot to crush and destroy the Jews.

The answer is that it would come back on Haman's own head. The king "…commanded by letter that the wicked scheme which Haman had devised against the Jews should come back upon his own head…" (Esther 9:25). The scheme Haman devised against the Jews was to come back upon his own head, friends. That's what the king's letter commanded.

The answer is False. The verse says, "Therefore these days are called Purim, from the word Pur." (Esther 9:26). The name comes from the Pur, which verse 24 says is the lot, friends. It doesn't come from the gallows.

The answer is descendants. The Jews "…bound themselves to establish the custom that they and their descendants and all who join them should not fail to celebrate these two days…" So the children and grandchildren and all the ones after them are covered, friends. That's a family tradition built to last.

The answer is False. The text says these days "…should be remembered and celebrated by every generation, family, province, and city…" (Esther 9:28). It also says the memory should not "…fade from their descendants." This was a plan for remembering, friends, and it was meant to go on and on.

The answer is False. Mordecai sent the letters "…in order to confirm these days of Purim at their appointed time…" (Esther 9:31). The date was set, so no city picked its own, friends. Everyone was on the same calendar, from the nearest town to the farthest.

The answer is that the rules are written into the record. "So Esther’s decree confirmed these regulations about Purim, which were written into the record." (Esther 9:32). Queen Esther's word made it official, and then it went into writing, friends. Once something's in the record, it doesn't get lost like a recipe card in a drawer.

The answer is the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Media and Persia. The writer asks, "…are they not written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Media and Persia?" (Esther 10:2). That's the book the text names for Mordecai's accomplishments and the greatness to which the king had raised him, friends. His story is written there.
The answer is second only to King Xerxes. "…Mordecai the Jew was second only to King Xerxes…" (Esther 10:3). Only the king ranked above him, friends. That's the rank the text gives him.

The answer is True. Mordecai was "…seeking the good of his people and speaking peace to all his countrymen." (Esther 10:3). The same verse says he was second only to King Xerxes, friends. Both things are said of him, and that's a good look on a powerful man.
